questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose Milano because I wanted to go to a big city where there was an international environment. I wanted to go to Italy because of the nice weather, food, culture, language, travel opportunities and the people <3

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Best decision I have made so far! 10/10

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Italians are very helpful if you ask. Therefore, you may not receive all the information upon arrival that you are used to in Denmark but the answer is always one email away. The Erasmus office at the uni was very helpful and quick to respond.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Again I received info from the Erasmus office at my uni.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The Erasmus office was 10/10 always helpful and provided different deadlines/important things we had to remember. The uni/professors did not provide much information. But again, pro-tip: write an email. Everything is less formal and more relaxed in Italy.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: The uni dorms har all located off-campus around 35-40 min. from the city center. But the transportation system is good, so no need to worry about that.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is worth knowing that the uni only provides 'shared rooms' for Erasmus students. Therefore you have to share a room with another person.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had a good experience but I was really lucky because I never got a roommate. The prices for the shared rooms are really affordable, so I think it is worth looking into, if you want to save some money on that front and use it for other things like travel/going out.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The registration proces for the courses was easy, after I wrote an email to the Erasmus office. I would 10/10 recommend doing that. Because the professors usually don't explain the uni's website/online platforms to Erasmus students.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration itself is easy and you have plenty of opportunities to change courses within the first couple of weeks. You just have to find the course, ECTS, professor and then write it in the UNIMIA online platform, where you also register for exams and so on.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can write to the Erasmus office or directly to the faculty. But I think it was difficult to find where I should write to the faculty, because they use an online platform for communication.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was successful in registering. Although one course was cancelled because the professor had become sick, so it had to find another course.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Look at different courses that might interest you and then write them down. Thereafter, look them up in the uni's calendar, so you can see if the time schedules clash or not. Sometimes the professors allow you to attend their course even though you are not able to attend every class every week, because you maybe have a different course at that time. I would recommend that you try and have no classes on either monday or friday, if you want to be able to travel for longer/long weekends :) Also look out for what kind of exams the courses have, because some exams are considerably easier than others. If the courses say that attendance is 'mandatory', that does not mean that you have to write your name or check-in every time you go to class. For some courses you have to, for others the professors don't bother taking attendance even though it says that they do. So go to the classes and see what that professor does.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The academic level is lower than in Copenhagen and the courses are smaller. But the upside is that you will be able to learn a mix of things, because the courses often involve knowledge from other degrees like sociology, history, AI/tech and so on. And you will also have more time to get to know people/the country, because you don't have to read as much as in Copenhagen.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Level was lover than in Copenhagen.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching is more focused on you attending and asking questions. I did not have to buy any books because the professors provided all the reading material on the online platform Ariel. The written exams are by hand and the oral exams are in front of the people in your class.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Gender Justice (6 ECTS)
Comparative Labour Law (6 ECTS)
Artificial Intelligence, law issue and sustainable development (6 ECTS)
Public and Private Partnership for Sustainable Development (6 ECTS)
Environmental and Food Law (6 ECTS)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Courses I would recommend:
I would really recommend taking the course ' Comparative labour Law' with Marco Biasi. The course gives you a general overview of labour laws around the world and the history behind labour. The professor is very sweet, funny and accommodating and tries to make everyone feel good. The exam is either oral or multiple-choice (you get to choose).

I would also recommend taking Environmental and Food Law. It is a very interesting course built up by two different areas, with one professor teaching Food Law and one teaching Environmental law. The professor are good at involving the students and making it interesting with relevant reading material and you also learn a lot about the political side. Student who attend the classes get to write an assignment as their exam, while you can also choose to take a written exam. 

The courses Artificial Intelligence, law issue and sustainable development and Public and Private Partnership for Sustainable Development are interesting/practical enough for you to use some other the knowledge in the future. The exams are 'written exam with 3 questions' and for the other one it is a group powerpoint presentation.

Courses I DO NO RECOMMEND!: 
Do not take 'Gender Justice' with Costanza Nardocci. The course itself is very interesting and deals with a lot of politics and sociology. But the professor is very intimidating and degrading. She does not create a healthy environment for learning and does not answer your questions or emails. The exam is oral + 2 written assignments, she will not explain what you can expect to encounter in the exam and she will judge your performance based on her mood that day.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did not encounter any unexpected costs. The SU and Erasmus scholarship covered all my usual expense + the majority of my travel cost. But of course I used different amounts for travel, depending on where I went.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The food in the supermarket is around the same cost as in Denmark. Eating out is a bit cheaper than in Copenhagen and travelling is cheap, if you buy the train tickets/flight tickets around 2-4 weeks before.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The uni did not really have any non-academic opportunities.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The uni did not really have any non-academic opportunities.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you are interested in sports, join a WhatsApp groups chat through ESN, where people who have similar interests arrange training sessions. I would personally recommend going to the museums, going traveling through Italy and go to the ESN events. You will meet all of your friends through ESN and they also organise a lot of different non-academic activities.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go travelling! go out at night with your friends and eat some good italian pizza and pasta. I really recommend going for 1 day trips to Lake Como, Lake Garda, Torino, Bergamo, Venice. I went on a fantastic weekend trip to Firenze + Bologna and on another weekend trip to Palermo (Sicily) + Napoli. Would recommend!!! Loved Sicily <3

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was very easy. Italians are very polite but you have to be patient. They don't all speak English fluently, so be accommodating and try and learn some basic words/sentences, this will help you a lot.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go to the ESN events! you will meet the Italians that are volunteers/organizers there. That's how I got local friends. Otherwise, talk tot he Italians in your courses or rent a room in an apartment where other Italians live.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: When the uni or dorm writes that something is not possible, it usually is perfectly possible, but you will have to write/call several times in order to get it sorted. They don't want to do extra paperwork.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The relaxed attitude to life, the passionate way they speak to you and greet you.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
The Erasmus Office (Massimo) is your best friend. When in doubt write an email.
Remember to take 1-2 days off from ESN events and social things every week. It is so much fun to be social but you will get burnt out if you don't also prioritize relaxing. 
Travel at any opportunity, don't be afraid ti write into the ESN chat and ask people if they want to go out or travel somewhere. There are always people in the same situation as you <3

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Get the ATM travel card, it's only 22 euros pr. month for students and get the CartaFreccia on the Trenitalia website, for student discounts on quick trains.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends I gained from all over the world, the travelling/social events, and the new perspective on different countries in europe/world, which only underlines how privileged we are <3

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The hardest part was the first couple of days where you realise that you are ON YOUR OWN. But as soon as you find some friends (go the the ESN events), then you will see that everyone is on their own, but it is not as scary, when you have others to share/support you on your journey :)

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Don't overthink it <3 everything will work out :)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
